papers.cite: Morice, C. P., et al. (2021). An updated assessment of near-surface temperature change from 1850: the HadCRUT5 data set. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 126(3), e2019JD032361.
papers.version: Accepted manuscript (hosted by the Met Office)
papers.about: Introduces HadCRUT5, the Met Office/UEA global surface temperature record from 1850, and why its infilled version shows more recent warming.

papers.cite: Rohde, R. A., & Hausfather, Z. (2020). The Berkeley Earth Land/Ocean Temperature Record. Earth System Science Data, 12(4), 3469–3479.
papers.about: Describes the Berkeley Earth global record and compares it with HadCRUT, GISTEMP and other series.

papers.cite: Forster, P. M., et al. (2025). Indicators of Global Climate Change 2024: annual update of key indicators of the state of the climate system and human influence. Earth System Science Data, 17(6), 2641–2680.
papers.about: The annual IPCC-style update: emissions, concentrations, forcing, observed and human-induced warming, remaining carbon budget.

papers.cite: Kendon, M., et al. (2025). State of the UK Climate in 2024. International Journal of Climatology, 45(S1), e70010.
papers.about: The Met Office’s annual assessment of UK temperature, rainfall, sunshine, wind, sea level and phenology.

papers.cite: Legg, T., et al. (2025). An Update to the Central England Temperature Series – HadCET v2.1. Geoscience Data Journal, 12, e284.
papers.about: Documents the current version of the Central England Temperature series: stations, homogenisation and urban adjustment.

papers.cite: Christidis, N., McCarthy, M., & Stott, P. A. (2020). The increasing likelihood of temperatures above 30 to 40 °C in the United Kingdom. Nature Communications, 11, 3093.
papers.about: Attribution study on how human influence raises the chance of 30–40 °C days in the UK – published two years before the 40.3 °C record of July 2022.

papers.cite: Vautard, R., et al. (2023). Heat extremes in Western Europe increasing faster than simulated due to atmospheric circulation trends. Nature Communications, 14, 6803.
papers.about: Shows that Western European heat extremes rise faster than climate models simulate, partly due to circulation changes.

papers.cite: Perkins-Kirkpatrick, S. E., & Lewis, S. C. (2020). Increasing trends in regional heatwaves. Nature Communications, 11, 3357.
papers.about: Heatwave frequency, duration, intensity and cumulative heat by region since 1950.

papers.cite: Myhre, G., et al. (2019). Frequency of extreme precipitation increases extensively with event rareness under global warming. Scientific Reports, 9, 16063.
papers.about: Extreme daily precipitation becomes more frequent with warming – the rarer the event, the larger the increase.

papers.cite: Christidis, N., Mitchell, D., & Stott, P. A. (2023). Rapidly increasing likelihood of exceeding 50 °C in parts of the Mediterranean and the Middle East due to human influence. npj Climate and Atmospheric Science, 6, 45.
papers.about: Transfers the UK 40 °C method (B3) to 50 °C days in the Mediterranean and Middle East.

papers.cite: Zachariah, M., et al. (2023). Attribution of 2022 early-spring heatwave in India and Pakistan to climate change: lessons in assessing vulnerability and preparedness in reducing impacts. Environmental Research: Climate, 2(4).
papers.about: A rapid event-attribution study combined with a vulnerability and impact assessment.

papers.cite: Schumacher, D. L., et al. (2024). Detecting the human fingerprint in the summer 2022 western–central European soil drought. Earth System Dynamics, 15, 131–154.
papers.about: Drought attribution for the European summer of 2022 – the drought counterpart to the heat papers.

papers.cite: Shi, X., Beaulieu, C., Killick, R., & Lund, R. (2021). Changepoint Detection: An Analysis of the Central England Temperature Series. arXiv:2106.12180 (preprint).
papers.version: Preprint – not peer reviewed in this version
papers.about: Applies changepoint methods to the Central England Temperature series.

data.title: Central England Temperature – daily
data.cite: Met Office HadCET v2.1; Parker et al. (1992); Legg et al. (2025).
data.notes: Actual temperatures, not anomalies. The most recent values are provisional.

data.title: Central England Temperature – monthly
data.format: Text, wide (year × 12 months + annual), header lines
data.cite: Met Office HadCET v2.1; Manley (1974); Parker et al. (1992).
data.notes: The longest instrumental temperature series; needs reshaping from wide to long.

data.title: Global temperature anomalies – HadCRUT5
data.provider: Met Office / University of East Anglia
data.notes: Anomalies relative to 1961–1990 – other series use other baselines.

data.title: Global temperature anomalies – GISTEMP v4
data.format: CSV, wide (year × months + seasons), title line to skip
data.cite: GISTEMP Team (2026), GISS Surface Temperature Analysis v4; Lenssen et al.

data.title: Global temperature anomalies – Berkeley Earth
data.format: Text with long % comment header, whitespace-separated
data.notes: Marked “preliminary” by the provider; missing values coded as NaN.

data.title: Atmospheric CO₂ – Mauna Loa, monthly
data.cite: Lan, X., Tans, P. & Thoning, K. W., NOAA GML; Scripps Institution of Oceanography.
data.notes: December 2022 – July 2023 measured on Maunakea after the Mauna Loa eruption; negative values are placeholders.

data.title: Sea-ice extent, Arctic and Antarctic – daily
data.format: CSV with a units row under the header
data.cite: Fetterer, F., et al., Sea Ice Index, Version 4 (G02135), NSIDC.
data.notes: Every other day until mid-1987 and a gap in 1987–88 – good for irregular time series.

data.title: UK station records – Oxford, Durham, Sutton Bonington
data.format: Text, header lines; tmax, tmin, air frost, rain, sun
data.notes: Codes to clean: --- missing, * estimated, # sensor type, “Provisional” rows. The best file for a data-cleaning test.

data.title: UK mean temperature and rainfall – national series
data.notes: Areal averages for the UK; --- marks missing seasonal values.

data.title: Global air temperature – daily (ERA5)
data.provider: Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF (Climate Pulse)
data.notes: Anomalies relative to 1991–2020; the last weeks are preliminary (ERA5T).

data.title: CO₂ and greenhouse-gas emissions by country
data.cite: Our World in Data, based on the Global Carbon Project (Friedlingstein et al., 2025).
data.notes: Contains aggregates (World, Europe, income groups) that must be filtered out before comparing countries. 20 MB – may be too large to upload to Copilot in one piece.
